title: Many US adults are skipping parenting or having fewer kids - and its forcing schools to close
author: Berger, Eric
summary: Eric Berger reports on the structural demographic shift reshaping American public education as the US fertility rate drops from 3.7 births per woman in 1960 to 1.6 today. School districts across the nation are closing buildings due to enrollment collapse rather than academic failure, with fixed infrastructure costs creating financial crises. The article documents how funding mechanisms tied to student enrollment leave districts unable to maintain aging physical plants.
points: Fertility decline is now reshaping public education in real time, with districts closing schools not due to failure but due to insufficient students.
School enrollment fell by 1.1 million students in 2020 alone, with many never returning, creating cascading funding problems.
Memphis-Shelby County saw enrollment drop by over 10,000 students between 2014-2024, forcing five immediate closures and considering 15 more.
Fixed building costs remain constant while funding follows declining enrollment, creating unsustainable budget gaps and deferred maintenance crises.
Demographic decline is not primarily an education issue; it reflects a deeper civilizational reorientation toward lower fertility as a cultural norm.
quotes: Fewer people are having children. In 1960, the fertility rate was 3.7 births per woman. Today it is about 1.6. That decline is now reshaping public education.
School districts across the country are closing buildings, not because the schools are failing, but because there are not enough students.
Funding follows students, but buildings still require the same fixed costs.
This is not just an education issue. It is what demographic decline looks like in real time.” Archived from The Guardian on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
